So deleting it still elaborates. I checked the reduction and it is mathematically sound. Let A be the path component of p in U and A' the path component of p in V. Since hI holds and p ∈ U∩V, U∩V ⊆ A∩A', and since A ⊆ U and A' ⊆ V, A∩A' = U∩V. Take a path γ from p in X. By hcover and a Lebesgue number, γ splits into pieces, each lying in U or in V. A junction between a U-piece and a V-piece lies in U∩V ⊆ A∩A'. By induction, each U-piece stays in A and each V-piece stays in A'. So the path component PC of p equals A∪A'. Then U∩PC = A: a point of U∩PC that lies in A' lies in U∩V ⊆ A. Likewise V∩PC = A'. So A and A' are relatively open in PC. They are path-connected, they cover PC, and their intersection U∩V is path-connected, so the theorem with all its hypotheses applies to PC with the cover A, A'. Loops at p and homotopies between them have path-connected images containing p. So π₁(A,p)→π₁(U,p), π₁(A',p)→π₁(V,p) and π₁(PC,p)→π₁(X,p) are isomorphisms, and all the inclusion squares commute. Hence existence and uniqueness of φ carry over, and the compatibility hypothesis carries over too. I found no degenerate-case counterexample, because p makes U∩V nonempty. Given hcover, hI and p ∈ U∩V, the path component PC of p is the union of A (the path component of p in U) and A' (the path component of p in V). A and A' are relatively open in PC because A = U∩PC and A' = V∩PC. They are path-connected, and their intersection U∩V is path-connected. The inclusions A→U, A'→V and PC→X induce isomorphisms on π₁ at p, so the universal property for X, U and V follows from the theorem applied to PC, A and A'.
